results.reason: Issue 1 quotes MSA §3.2's nationwide scope covering all warehousing, freight and delivery services. It contrasts this with Term Sheet §§4.1–4.2, which limit exclusivity to NYC-metro last-mile delivery. It then gives replacement language narrowing exclusivity to that scope.

Issue 2 explains that MSA §11.3 makes Customer's §10.2 indemnity apply 'without limitation' while Provider's §10.1 indemnity stays under the §11.1 cap. It describes the resulting asymmetric uncapped exposure. It recommends deleting the first sentence of §11.3 or using a symmetrical super-cap.

Issue 5 identifies that DPA §9.1 selects Delaware law and Wilmington courts, conflicting with MSA §18.1's New York law and forum. It notes that MSA §2.3 ranks the DPA first. It recommends replacing DPA §9.1 with a reference to MSA §18, which conforms it to New York.

Issue 4 identifies the three-year auto-renewal and the 15-day notice window. It explains the lock-in, including roughly $6.6M in further fees and continued exclusivity. It recommends one-year renewals, notice at least 60 days before expiry, or deleting auto-renewal.

Issue 6 identifies that MSA §17.4 restricts only Customer and that SOW §8.2 lets Provider assign without consent. It explains the risks of transfer to an unvetted party or a competitor. It recommends a mutual consent clause with a competitor restriction.
Issue 5 states that MSA §2.3 ranks the DPA first, above the MSA and SOW. Issue 1 separately states that the MSA outranks the SOW under §2.3.
Issue 3 quotes MSA §11.1 as capping liability at 'the fees paid or payable in the 12 months before the claim.'

The response is a memo addressed to the Supervising Partner. Each major issue has 'Where', 'Why it matters' and 'Recommended fix' headings. The cleanup items are in a table with document/section, issue and fix columns.
Issues are tiered by importance (Tier 1: must fix; Tier 2: important; Tier 3: cleanup). Section 3 lists items to raise with the client before the next turn.
The response treats the Delaware/New York governing-law split as a real conflict, with the DPA prevailing. It does not claim New York law controls data disputes or that the documents are consistent.
The response states expressly that the exclusivity clause is far broader than the Term Sheet scope.
